title: Common Cold: Symptoms and Overview
content: The common cold is a mild viral infection of the nose and throat, most often caused by rhinoviruses. Typical symptoms include a runny or stuffy nose, sneezing, sore throat, mild cough, mild headache, and general tiredness. Fever is usually absent or very low-grade in adults, though children may run a higher fever. Symptoms typically build over 1-3 days, peak around day 3-5, and resolve within 7-10 days. Most colds do not require medical treatment and resolve on their own with rest and fluids.

title: Influenza (Flu): Symptoms and Overview
content: Influenza is a contagious respiratory illness caused by influenza viruses. Unlike a cold, flu symptoms usually begin abruptly and are more severe: high fever (often 101-104°F), chills, body aches, headache, fatigue that can be severe, dry cough, sore throat, and nasal congestion. Symptoms typically last about a week, though fatigue can linger longer. Most healthy people recover without complications, but flu can lead to serious complications like pneumonia in young children, older adults, pregnant women, and people with chronic conditions. Annual flu vaccination is the most effective prevention.

title: Migraine Headache: Symptoms and Overview
content: A migraine is a moderate to severe headache, often on one side of the head, described as throbbing or pulsing. Common accompanying symptoms include nausea, vomiting, and extreme sensitivity to light and sound. Some people experience an 'aura' beforehand — visual disturbances like flashing lights or zigzag lines. Attacks can last 4 to 72 hours if untreated. Common triggers include stress, certain foods (aged cheese, red wine, caffeine), hormonal changes, lack of sleep, and bright lights. Migraines differ from tension headaches, which cause a dull, pressing pain on both sides of the head without nausea or light sensitivity.

title: Tension Headache: Symptoms and Overview
content: Tension-type headaches are the most common form of headache, causing a dull, aching sensation on both sides of the head, often described as a tight band around the head. Unlike migraines, tension headaches do not typically cause nausea, vomiting, or significant sensitivity to light. Common triggers include stress, poor posture, eye strain, dehydration, and lack of sleep. They usually respond well to rest, hydration, and over-the-counter pain relief such as acetaminophen or ibuprofen.

title: Dengue Fever: Symptoms and Overview
content: Dengue fever is a mosquito-borne viral infection common in tropical and subtropical regions. Symptoms typically appear 4-10 days after being bitten and include sudden high fever, severe headache (often behind the eyes), muscle and joint pain (sometimes called 'breakbone fever'), nausea, vomiting, skin rash, and mild bleeding such as nosebleeds or bruising. Most cases resolve within 1-2 weeks, but a small percentage can progress to severe dengue, a medical emergency with warning signs like severe abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, and bleeding. There is no specific antiviral treatment; management is supportive.

title: Malaria: Symptoms and Overview
content: Malaria is a mosquito-borne parasitic disease caused by Plasmodium parasites, common in tropical regions. Symptoms usually appear 10-15 days after an infective mosquito bite and include high fever with chills and sweating (often in cycles), headache, muscle aches, fatigue, nausea, and vomiting. Fever patterns can be cyclical, recurring every 24-72 hours depending on the parasite species. Malaria is a medical emergency requiring prompt diagnosis and treatment, as it can progress rapidly to severe illness, especially in children and pregnant women. Artemisinin-based combination therapies are the frontline treatment.

title: Typhoid Fever: Symptoms and Overview
content: Typhoid fever is a bacterial infection caused by Salmonella Typhi, spread through contaminated food and water. Symptoms develop gradually over 1-3 weeks and include sustained high fever that rises in a stepwise pattern, headache, weakness and fatigue, abdominal pain, constipation or diarrhea, and sometimes a rash of flat, rose-colored spots (rose spots) on the trunk. Untreated typhoid can lead to serious complications including intestinal perforation, so prompt antibiotic treatment is important. Vaccination is recommended for travellers to endemic regions.

title: Urinary Tract Infection (UTI): Symptoms and Overview
content: A urinary tract infection (UTI) is a bacterial infection anywhere in the urinary system — kidneys, ureters, bladder, or urethra. Lower UTIs (bladder/urethra) are most common, especially in women. Common symptoms include a strong, persistent urge to urinate, a burning sensation when urinating, passing frequent small amounts of urine, cloudy or strong-smelling urine, and pelvic pain in women. If the infection spreads to the kidneys (pyelonephritis), symptoms can include fever, chills, back or side pain, nausea, and vomiting — this requires prompt medical attention. Uncomplicated UTIs are treated with a short course of antibiotics.

title: Gastritis: Symptoms and Overview
content: Gastritis is inflammation of the stomach lining, often caused by infection with Helicobacter pylori bacteria, excessive alcohol use, or long-term use of NSAIDs (non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs) such as ibuprofen or aspirin. Symptoms include a gnawing or burning pain in the upper abdomen (epigastric pain), nausea, vomiting, a feeling of fullness after eating only a small amount, bloating, and loss of appetite. Some people have no symptoms at all. Diagnosis often involves endoscopy or H. pylori testing. Chronic untreated gastritis can increase the risk of stomach ulcers and, with H. pylori infection, stomach cancer.

title: Food Poisoning: Symptoms and Overview
content: Food poisoning results from eating contaminated food, usually caused by bacteria (Salmonella, E. coli, Listeria, Campylobacter), viruses (norovirus), or parasites. Symptoms typically begin within hours to a few days of eating contaminated food and include nausea, vomiting, watery or bloody diarrhea, abdominal cramps, and sometimes fever. Most cases resolve within a few days with rest and oral rehydration. Severe cases with high fever, bloody stool, signs of dehydration, or symptoms lasting more than three days need medical attention. Vulnerable groups — pregnant women, elderly, immunocompromised — should seek care earlier.

title: Asthma: Symptoms and Overview
content: Asthma is a chronic condition causing inflammation and narrowing of the airways. Common symptoms include shortness of breath, chest tightness, wheezing (a high-pitched whistling sound when breathing), and coughing, often worse at night or early morning, or triggered by exercise, cold air, allergens, or respiratory infections. Symptom severity varies widely between people and can range from mild and occasional to severe and frequent, sometimes leading to asthma attacks that require emergency treatment. Long-term control medications (inhaled corticosteroids) reduce inflammation; short-acting bronchodilators (rescue inhalers) relieve acute symptoms.

title: Hypertension (High Blood Pressure): Symptoms and Overview
content: Hypertension is often called a 'silent condition' because it typically causes no noticeable symptoms, even when blood pressure readings are dangerously high. Most people find out they have high blood pressure through a routine check. In rare cases of very severe hypertension (hypertensive crisis), symptoms can include severe headache, shortness of breath, nosebleeds, and chest pain. Because it is usually symptomless, regular blood pressure checks are the main way it is detected. Untreated, it significantly raises the risk of heart attack, stroke, heart failure, and kidney disease. Lifestyle changes (diet, exercise, reduced salt and alcohol) and antihypertensive medications are the main treatments.

title: Type 2 Diabetes: Symptoms and Overview
content: Type 2 diabetes often develops gradually and symptoms can be subtle at first. Common signs include increased thirst (polydipsia), frequent urination (polyuria), increased hunger (polyphagia), unexplained weight loss, fatigue, blurred vision, slow-healing sores, and frequent infections (especially skin, gum, or bladder). Some people have no noticeable symptoms for years before diagnosis, which is why routine blood sugar (HbA1c or fasting glucose) screening is important, especially for people with obesity, a family history of diabetes, or a sedentary lifestyle. Management combines lifestyle changes, oral medications, and sometimes insulin.

title: Iron Deficiency Anemia: Symptoms and Overview
content: Iron deficiency anemia is the most common type of anemia worldwide, occurring when the body does not have enough iron to produce adequate hemoglobin — the protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen. Common symptoms include fatigue and weakness, pale or sallow skin, shortness of breath on exertion, dizziness, cold hands and feet, brittle nails, headache, and a fast or irregular heartbeat. In some cases, people develop pica — cravings for non-food substances like ice or dirt. Symptoms often develop slowly. Common causes include blood loss (heavy periods, gastrointestinal bleeding), poor dietary iron intake, and increased needs during pregnancy. Treatment involves iron supplementation and addressing the underlying cause.

title: Allergic Rhinitis (Hay Fever): Symptoms and Overview
content: Allergic rhinitis is an immune-mediated inflammation of the nasal passages triggered by allergens such as pollen, dust mites, mold spores, or pet dander. Symptoms include sneezing, runny or stuffy nose (rhinorrhea or nasal congestion), itchy and watery eyes (allergic conjunctivitis), itchy throat or ears, and postnasal drip. Unlike a cold, allergic rhinitis does not cause fever and symptoms can persist for as long as the person is exposed to the trigger — sometimes lasting weeks during pollen seasons. Treatment options include antihistamines, intranasal corticosteroid sprays (most effective), allergen avoidance, and, for long-term desensitization, allergen immunotherapy.

title: Sinusitis: Symptoms and Overview
content: Sinusitis is inflammation of the lining of the sinuses — the air-filled spaces behind the cheekbones, forehead, and nose — often following a viral upper respiratory infection (common cold) or triggered by allergies or a bacterial infection. Symptoms include facial pain or pressure (especially around the eyes, cheeks, and forehead), nasal congestion, thick nasal or postnasal discharge (yellow or green), reduced sense of smell or taste, headache, and sometimes mild fever and fatigue. Acute sinusitis usually resolves within 2-4 weeks; symptoms lasting longer than 12 weeks may indicate chronic sinusitis. Most acute cases are viral and do not require antibiotics.

title: Conjunctivitis (Pink Eye): Symptoms and Overview
content: Conjunctivitis is inflammation of the conjunctiva — the thin transparent membrane covering the white of the eye and the inner surface of the eyelids — commonly caused by viral or bacterial infection, or allergies. Symptoms include redness in the white of the eye, itchiness, a gritty feeling (like sand in the eye), discharge (watery in viral and allergic; thick, sticky, and pus-like in bacterial infection), and crusting of the eyelashes especially in the morning. Viral conjunctivitis is highly contagious and often accompanies a cold; it usually resolves within 1-2 weeks without treatment. Bacterial conjunctivitis may be treated with antibiotic eye drops.

title: Chickenpox (Varicella): Symptoms and Overview
content: Chickenpox (varicella) is a highly contagious viral infection caused by the varicella-zoster virus. Symptoms typically begin with mild fever, tiredness, headache, and loss of appetite, followed 1-2 days later by a characteristic itchy rash that starts as red spots, develops into fluid-filled blisters (vesicles), and eventually crusts over. New spots can appear over several days, so the rash often shows lesions at different stages simultaneously. The rash typically appears first on the face, scalp, and chest and spreads. Most cases in healthy children are mild and resolve within 1-2 weeks. After recovery, the virus remains dormant in nerve tissue and can reactivate later in life as shingles (herpes zoster).

title: Measles: Symptoms and Overview
content: Measles is a highly contagious viral infection caused by the measles morbillivirus. Early symptoms (prodrome) include high fever, persistent cough, runny nose (coryza), and red, watery eyes (conjunctivitis), appearing 10-14 days after exposure. Small white spots with a bluish-white center on a red background, called Koplik spots, may appear inside the mouth 1-2 days before the rash. A few days later, a red, blotchy, non-itchy rash typically starts on the face and spreads downward over the body. Measles can lead to serious complications including pneumonia, encephalitis, and blindness, particularly in malnourished children or those under five, making vaccination with the MMR vaccine essential.

title: Pneumonia: Symptoms and Overview
content: Pneumonia is an infection that inflames the air sacs (alveoli) in one or both lungs, which may fill with fluid or pus. It can be caused by bacteria (Streptococcus pneumoniae is most common), viruses (including influenza and SARS-CoV-2), or fungi. Symptoms include cough (often producing green, yellow, or bloody phlegm), fever, chills, shortness of breath, chest pain that worsens with breathing or coughing, fatigue, and in severe cases or in older adults, confusion. Community-acquired pneumonia is the most common type. Hospitalization may be needed for those with severe symptoms, very young children, elderly patients, or those with weakened immune systems.

title: Bronchitis: Symptoms and Overview
content: Bronchitis is inflammation of the bronchial tubes — the airways that carry air to the lungs — typically caused by a viral infection. Acute bronchitis symptoms include a persistent cough (which may produce clear, yellow, or greenish mucus), chest discomfort, mild fever, fatigue, and shortness of breath. The cough can linger for several weeks even after other symptoms resolve, because the inflamed airways take time to heal. Most cases of acute bronchitis are viral and resolve without antibiotics. Chronic bronchitis, a form of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), involves a persistent productive cough lasting at least three months over two consecutive years, typically caused by long-term smoking.

title: GERD (Acid Reflux): Symptoms and Overview
content: Gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) is a chronic condition that occurs when stomach acid frequently flows back (refluxes) into the esophagus, irritating its lining. Common symptoms include heartburn (a burning sensation in the chest, often after eating or when lying down), regurgitation of food or sour liquid into the throat, difficulty swallowing (dysphagia), chest pain, chronic cough, hoarseness, and a sensation of a lump in the throat (globus). Symptoms often worsen when lying down or bending over after meals. Lifestyle modifications (smaller meals, avoiding trigger foods like fatty or spicy foods, not lying down after eating, elevating the head of the bed) help. Medications include antacids, H2 blockers, and proton pump inhibitors (PPIs).

title: Irritable Bowel Syndrome (IBS): Symptoms and Overview
content: Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) is a common functional gastrointestinal disorder affecting the large intestine. It is characterized by abdominal pain or cramping that is often relieved by a bowel movement, bloating, gas, and changes in bowel habits — either diarrhea-predominant (IBS-D), constipation-predominant (IBS-C), or alternating between both (IBS-M). Symptoms often flare up after eating certain foods (fatty foods, caffeine, alcohol, dairy) or during stress. IBS does not cause permanent damage to the intestines or increase the risk of colorectal cancer, but it can significantly affect quality of life. Management includes dietary changes (low-FODMAP diet), stress management, and medications targeting specific symptoms.

title: Hypothyroidism: Symptoms and Overview
content: Hypothyroidism occurs when the thyroid gland does not produce enough thyroid hormone, slowing the body's metabolism. The most common cause is Hashimoto's thyroiditis, an autoimmune condition. Symptoms develop gradually and include persistent fatigue, unexplained weight gain, cold intolerance, dry skin, hair thinning or loss, brittle nails, constipation, muscle weakness or aches, joint pain, depression, cognitive slowing ('brain fog'), slowed heart rate (bradycardia), and a puffy face. Because symptoms are often subtle and overlap with many other conditions, a blood test measuring TSH (thyroid-stimulating hormone) and free T4 is needed to confirm the diagnosis. Treatment is daily oral levothyroxine (synthetic T4).

title: Hyperthyroidism: Symptoms and Overview
content: Hyperthyroidism occurs when the thyroid gland produces too much thyroid hormone, accelerating the body's metabolism. The most common cause is Graves' disease, an autoimmune condition. Symptoms include unexplained weight loss despite normal or increased appetite, rapid or irregular heartbeat (palpitations, atrial fibrillation), increased sweating and heat intolerance, nervousness, anxiety, or irritability, tremors (fine trembling) in the hands or fingers, difficulty sleeping, and frequent bowel movements. Some people also develop an enlarged thyroid gland (goiter), and Graves' disease can cause distinctive eye changes (Graves' ophthalmopathy) — protrusion, redness, or double vision. Treatment options include antithyroid medications, radioiodine therapy, and surgery.

title: Kidney Stones: Symptoms and Overview
content: Kidney stones (nephrolithiasis or urolithiasis) are hard crystalline deposits of minerals and salts — most commonly calcium oxalate — that form inside the kidneys. Small stones may pass through the urinary tract without symptoms. Larger stones can cause severe, sharp, cramping pain (renal colic) in the side and back, below the ribs, that may radiate to the lower abdomen and groin as the stone moves. Other symptoms include pain or burning during urination, blood in the urine (hematuria — pink, red, or brown), nausea, vomiting, and a frequent urge to urinate. Stones that block urine flow or are accompanied by fever require urgent medical attention. Treatment depends on size — small stones pass with hydration; larger stones may need lithotripsy, ureteroscopy, or surgery.

title: Gallstones: Symptoms and Overview
content: Gallstones are hardened deposits — composed of cholesterol or bilirubin — that form in the gallbladder. Most gallstones cause no symptoms and are discovered incidentally. When a stone blocks the bile duct, it causes a 'biliary colic' attack: sudden and rapidly intensifying pain in the upper right abdomen or center of the abdomen (epigastric pain), sometimes radiating to the right shoulder blade or right shoulder, nausea, and vomiting, often triggered after eating fatty meals. Attacks can last from a few minutes to several hours. If a stone causes a persistent blockage and infection (cholecystitis or cholangitis), symptoms include fever, jaundice (yellowing of the skin and eyes), and persistent severe pain — these require prompt medical attention. Laparoscopic cholecystectomy (gallbladder removal) is the definitive treatment.

title: Appendicitis: Symptoms and Overview
content: Appendicitis is inflammation of the appendix — a small pouch attached to the large intestine — and is a surgical emergency. Classic symptoms begin with pain around the navel (umbilicus) that progressively shifts to the lower right abdomen (McBurney's point) over several hours and worsens with movement, coughing, or deep breathing. Accompanying symptoms include loss of appetite, nausea, vomiting, low-grade fever (38-39°C), and abdominal rigidity or guarding. In some cases the appendix perforates, causing more widespread, severe abdominal pain and higher fever. Anyone with suspected appendicitis should seek emergency care immediately — surgical removal (appendectomy) is the standard treatment.

title: Osteoarthritis: Symptoms and Overview
content: Osteoarthritis (OA) is the most common form of arthritis, caused by the progressive breakdown of articular cartilage in joints. Symptoms include joint pain that worsens with activity and improves with rest, morning stiffness that lasts less than 30 minutes (distinguishing it from inflammatory arthritis), reduced range of motion, a grating, crackling, or popping sensation (crepitus) when using the joint, bony enlargements at joint margins (osteophytes), and swelling. OA most commonly affects the hands (especially the base of the thumb and finger end joints), knees, hips, and spine, and typically develops gradually over years. Management includes exercise, physical therapy, weight loss (for weight-bearing joints), analgesics (acetaminophen, NSAIDs), and joint replacement surgery for severe cases.

title: Rheumatoid Arthritis: Symptoms and Overview
content: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a chronic autoimmune condition in which the immune system mistakenly attacks the synovial lining of joints, causing persistent inflammation. Symptoms include tender, warm, swollen joints — characteristically affecting joints symmetrically on both sides of the body — joint stiffness that is worse in the mornings (lasting more than 30 minutes) or after periods of inactivity, fatigue, low-grade fever, and loss of appetite. Unlike osteoarthritis, RA commonly affects the small joints of the hands and feet first. RA can also cause systemic complications affecting the heart, lungs, skin, and eyes. Treatment aims at disease remission using disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (DMARDs) such as methotrexate and biologic agents.

title: Depression: Symptoms and Overview
content: Major depressive disorder (MDD) is a mood disorder characterized by persistent low mood and a loss of interest or pleasure in activities (anhedonia) that interferes with daily functioning. Core symptoms include persistent sad, empty, or hopeless mood; loss of interest in hobbies or activities once enjoyed; changes in appetite or weight (either increased or decreased); sleep disturbances (insomnia or hypersomnia); fatigue or low energy; feelings of worthlessness or excessive or inappropriate guilt; difficulty thinking, concentrating, or making decisions; psychomotor agitation or slowing; and, in severe cases, recurrent thoughts of death, suicidal ideation, or a suicide attempt. Symptoms must be present most of the day, nearly every day, for at least two weeks. Treatment includes psychotherapy (especially cognitive-behavioral therapy), antidepressant medications, or a combination. If you are having thoughts of suicide, please contact a crisis helpline or emergency services immediately.

title: Anxiety Disorder: Symptoms and Overview
content: Generalized anxiety disorder (GAD) involves excessive, persistent, and difficult-to-control worry about multiple areas of life — work, health, family, finances — out of proportion to actual risks. Psychological symptoms include restlessness or feeling on edge, difficulty concentrating, irritability, and mind going blank. Physical symptoms include muscle tension, fatigue, headaches, and sleep disturbances (difficulty falling or staying asleep). Panic disorder involves recurrent, unexpected panic attacks — sudden surges of intense fear with heart racing, sweating, trembling, shortness of breath, chest tightness, dizziness, and a sense of unreality or impending doom. Anxiety disorders are considered clinically significant when symptoms are persistent (most days for six months or more for GAD) and cause meaningful interference with daily life. Treatment includes cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT) and medications (SSRIs, SNRIs).

title: Insomnia: Symptoms and Overview
content: Insomnia is a sleep disorder characterized by persistent difficulty falling asleep, staying asleep, waking too early, or non-restorative sleep, despite adequate opportunity and circumstances for sleep. Daytime consequences include fatigue, low energy, impaired concentration or memory, irritability, mood disturbances, and increased errors or accidents. Acute insomnia is often triggered by stress or a life event and lasts days to weeks. Chronic insomnia occurs at least three nights per week for at least three months. Common contributing factors include anxiety, depression, poor sleep hygiene, irregular schedules, caffeine, screen use before bed, and certain medications. Cognitive-behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) is the most effective long-term treatment; sleep medications may be used short-term.

title: Vitamin D Deficiency: Symptoms and Overview
content: Vitamin D deficiency often causes no obvious symptoms, especially when mild. When symptoms do occur, they can include fatigue, bone pain, muscle weakness or aches, mood changes (including depression), and impaired wound healing. Severe, prolonged deficiency in children causes rickets — softening and weakening of bones leading to skeletal deformities (bowed legs, delayed tooth eruption). In adults, severe deficiency causes osteomalacia — softening of the bones that causes bone pain, muscle weakness, and increased fracture risk. Diagnosis requires a blood test measuring serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D; levels below 20 ng/mL (50 nmol/L) are considered deficient. Risk factors include limited sun exposure, dark skin pigmentation, older age, obesity, malabsorption syndromes, and certain medications. Treatment involves vitamin D3 supplementation.

title: Eczema (Atopic Dermatitis): Symptoms and Overview
content: Atopic dermatitis (eczema) is a chronic, relapsing inflammatory skin condition that is part of the 'atopic triad' along with asthma and allergic rhinitis. Symptoms include intense itching (pruritus), often worse at night; dry, sensitive skin; red, inflamed, or brownish-gray patches; small fluid-filled bumps that weep when scratched; thickened, cracked, or scaly skin; and raw, swollen skin from scratching. In infants, eczema typically affects the face and scalp; in older children and adults, it tends to involve the creases of the elbows and knees, wrists, neck, and around the eyes. Flares are triggered by irritants (soaps, detergents), allergens (dust mites, pet dander), sweat, stress, and weather changes. Management includes emollients, topical corticosteroids, and avoiding triggers.

title: Psoriasis: Symptoms and Overview
content: Psoriasis is a chronic immune-mediated skin condition that accelerates the skin cell life cycle, causing cells to build up rapidly on the skin surface. The most common type, plaque psoriasis, presents as raised, red patches covered with thick, silvery-white scales (plaques), typically on the scalp, elbows, knees, and lower back. Other symptoms include dry, cracked skin that may bleed, itching, burning, or soreness, thickened, pitted, or ridged nails, and joint pain and swelling in psoriatic arthritis (affecting up to 30% of people with psoriasis). Symptoms often come and go in cycles, flaring for weeks or months then subsiding. Triggers include stress, infections, smoking, heavy alcohol consumption, and certain medications (beta-blockers, lithium). Treatment ranges from topical therapies to phototherapy and biologic agents for moderate-to-severe disease.

title: Vertigo: Symptoms and Overview
content: Vertigo is a sensation of spinning or rotation — as if you or your surroundings are moving when they are not — distinct from simple dizziness or lightheadedness. The most common cause is benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV), caused by calcium crystals (otoliths) displaced in the inner ear canals. Other causes include Menière's disease (fluid buildup in the inner ear, with episodic vertigo, tinnitus, and fluctuating hearing loss), vestibular neuritis (viral inflammation of the vestibular nerve), and, less commonly, central causes (cerebellar or brainstem disorders). Accompanying symptoms may include nausea, vomiting, loss of balance, nystagmus (involuntary eye movements), and, depending on cause, hearing changes or tinnitus. BPPV is effectively treated with particle-repositioning maneuvers (Epley maneuver).

title: Sciatica: Symptoms and Overview
content: Sciatica describes pain that radiates along the course of the sciatic nerve — from the lower back through the buttock and down the back of the leg, typically affecting only one side. It is most commonly caused by a herniated lumbar disc compressing one of the nerve roots that form the sciatic nerve, or by lumbar spinal stenosis or a bone spur. Symptoms include sharp, shooting, or burning pain that can extend from the lower back all the way to the calf or foot; numbness or tingling in the leg or foot; and muscle weakness in the affected limb. Pain often worsens with prolonged sitting, coughing, or sneezing, and improves when lying down. Most cases improve within 4-6 weeks with conservative management (physiotherapy, anti-inflammatories, activity modification).

title: Gout: Symptoms and Overview
content: Gout is a form of inflammatory arthritis caused by the deposition of monosodium urate crystals in a joint, resulting from elevated serum uric acid (hyperuricemia). A classic acute gout attack typically begins suddenly, often at night, causing severe, excruciating pain, swelling, redness, and warmth in the affected joint — most classically the first metatarsophalangeal joint (big toe), a condition called podagra. Other commonly affected joints include the ankles, knees, and wrists. Attacks typically peak within 24 hours and subside over days to two weeks even without treatment. Repeated attacks over years can lead to tophi (deposits of urate crystals under the skin) and joint damage. Acute attacks are treated with NSAIDs, colchicine, or corticosteroids; long-term management of hyperuricemia uses allopurinol or febuxostat.

title: Stroke: Symptoms, Recognition, and Emergency Response
content: A stroke occurs when blood supply to part of the brain is suddenly interrupted (ischemic stroke, ~85% of cases) or when a blood vessel in the brain ruptures (hemorrhagic stroke). The FAST acronym summarizes key warning signs: Face drooping (one side of the face drooping or numbness, uneven smile), Arm weakness (one arm weak or numb, drifts down when raised), Speech difficulty (slurred, garbled, or unable to speak), Time to call emergency services immediately. Other symptoms include sudden severe headache ('thunderclap headache'), sudden vision loss or double vision in one or both eyes, sudden dizziness, loss of balance or coordination. Stroke is a medical emergency — every minute of delayed treatment results in the loss of approximately 1.9 million neurons. Ischemic stroke is treated with IV tPA (clot-busting medication) if given within 4.5 hours.

title: Heart Attack (Myocardial Infarction): Symptoms and Emergency Response
content: A heart attack (myocardial infarction) occurs when blood flow to a part of the heart muscle is blocked, usually by a blood clot forming on a ruptured cholesterol plaque in a coronary artery. Classic symptoms include crushing, pressure-like or squeezing chest pain (angina) that may radiate to the left arm, jaw, neck, or back; shortness of breath; cold sweat; nausea; and lightheadedness. Women, elderly individuals, and people with diabetes may present with atypical symptoms: unusual fatigue, jaw or upper back pain, or indigestion-like discomfort without obvious chest pain. A heart attack is a medical emergency — call emergency services immediately, chew aspirin (if not allergic, 325 mg) while waiting, and do not drive yourself. Rapid restoration of blood flow through percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI / angioplasty) or thrombolysis saves heart muscle.

title: COVID-19: Symptoms and Overview
content: COVID-19 is a respiratory illness caused by the SARS-CoV-2 coronavirus. Symptoms range widely in severity — from asymptomatic to critical illness. Common symptoms include fever or chills, cough (usually dry), fatigue, muscle or body aches, headache, new loss of taste or smell (anosmia/ageusia — particularly characteristic of early variants), sore throat, runny nose, nausea or vomiting, and diarrhea. Shortness of breath or difficulty breathing, persistent chest pain, confusion, and inability to stay awake are warning signs of severe disease requiring immediate medical attention. High-risk groups for severe disease include older adults, those with obesity, diabetes, heart disease, chronic lung disease, or immunosuppression. Prevention includes vaccination, wearing masks in high-risk settings, and good hand hygiene. Antiviral medications (e.g., nirmatrelvir-ritonavir) are available for high-risk individuals with early infection.

title: Tuberculosis (TB): Symptoms and Overview
content: Tuberculosis (TB) is a bacterial infection caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, primarily affecting the lungs (pulmonary TB) but capable of infecting any organ. Active pulmonary TB symptoms include a persistent cough lasting three or more weeks (often producing blood-tinged sputum), chest pain, night sweats, fever, unintentional weight loss, fatigue, and loss of appetite. Latent TB infection (LTBI) is asymptomatic — the bacteria are dormant and the person is not infectious, but can reactivate. TB spreads through the air when a person with active pulmonary TB coughs, sneezes, or speaks. Diagnosis involves tuberculin skin test (TST), interferon-gamma release assays (IGRAs), chest X-ray, and sputum culture. Treatment requires at least 6 months of combination antibiotic therapy (isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide, ethambutol).

title: Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD): Symptoms and Overview
content: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is a chronic, progressive lung disease characterized by persistent respiratory symptoms and airflow limitation, primarily caused by long-term cigarette smoking (90% of cases) or exposure to noxious particles or gases. COPD encompasses chronic bronchitis (persistent productive cough for at least 3 months in 2 consecutive years) and emphysema (destruction of the alveolar walls). Main symptoms are progressive breathlessness (dyspnea) on exertion, chronic cough (often productive in the morning), regular sputum production, wheezing, and chest tightness. Frequent respiratory infections and 'exacerbations' (acute worsening episodes) are common. Diagnosis is confirmed with spirometry. Management includes smoking cessation (most important), bronchodilators, inhaled corticosteroids, pulmonary rehabilitation, and supplemental oxygen for severe cases.

title: Celiac Disease: Symptoms and Overview
content: Celiac disease is an autoimmune disorder in which ingestion of gluten — a protein found in wheat, barley, and rye — triggers an immune response that damages the lining of the small intestine, impairing nutrient absorption. Gastrointestinal symptoms include chronic diarrhea or loose stools, bloating, gas, abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting. However, many people present with non-gastrointestinal ('silent' or atypical) symptoms: iron-deficiency anemia unresponsive to oral iron, fatigue, bone or joint pain, osteoporosis, peripheral neuropathy, skin rash (dermatitis herpetiformis — a blistering, intensely itchy rash), depression, headaches, and infertility. Diagnosis requires serologic testing (anti-tTG IgA antibody) and small intestinal biopsy. The only effective treatment is a strict, lifelong gluten-free diet.

title: Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS): Symptoms and Overview
content: Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) is a common hormonal disorder among women of reproductive age, characterized by excess androgen levels, irregular or absent menstrual cycles, and polycystic ovaries on ultrasound (though not all three features need be present for diagnosis). Symptoms include irregular, infrequent, or prolonged menstrual periods; excess androgen signs (hirsutism — excess hair on the face, chest, or back; acne; male-pattern hair thinning); polycystic ovaries visible on ultrasound; and difficulty getting pregnant (infertility). PCOS is also strongly associated with insulin resistance, weight gain, and metabolic syndrome, increasing long-term risk of type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease. Management depends on the presenting concern: hormonal contraception for cycle regulation, anti-androgens for hirsutism, and ovulation induction for fertility.

title: Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD): Symptoms and Overview
content: Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is the gradual, irreversible loss of kidney function over months to years. Early-stage CKD usually has no symptoms and is detected through blood tests (elevated serum creatinine, reduced eGFR) and urine tests (proteinuria). As kidney function declines, symptoms can include fatigue, swelling in the legs and ankles (edema), shortness of breath, nausea, decreased appetite, persistent itching, muscle cramps, urinating more or less than usual, difficulty sleeping, and cognitive impairment. Hypertension and diabetes are the leading causes of CKD worldwide. Management aims to slow progression (blood pressure control, blood sugar control, ACE inhibitors or ARBs), manage complications (anemia, bone disease), and prepare for renal replacement therapy (dialysis or kidney transplantation) when kidneys fail.

title: Vitamin B12 Deficiency: Symptoms and Overview
content: Vitamin B12 (cobalamin) is essential for red blood cell formation, DNA synthesis, and neurological function. Deficiency — most common in older adults, strict vegetarians/vegans, and people with malabsorption (pernicious anemia, Crohn's disease, gastric bypass) — causes a broad range of symptoms. Hematological symptoms include megaloblastic anemia: fatigue, weakness, pale or slightly yellow skin, and shortness of breath. Neurological symptoms (which can occur even without anemia) include numbness or tingling in the hands and feet (peripheral neuropathy), balance problems, difficulty walking, vision disturbances, and memory problems or cognitive decline. Psychiatric symptoms include depression, mood changes, and, in severe cases, psychosis. Diagnosis is by serum B12 level, with methylmalonic acid or homocysteine as confirmatory markers. Treatment involves oral or intramuscular B12 supplementation.

title: Sepsis: Recognition and Emergency Response
content: Sepsis is a life-threatening medical emergency caused by the body's extreme, dysregulated response to an infection — the immune system begins damaging the body's own tissues and organs. It can arise from any infection (pneumonia, UTI, abdominal infection, skin infection) and can progress rapidly to septic shock and multiple organ failure. Warning signs include: very high or very low body temperature, heart rate over 90 beats/minute, breathing rate over 20 breaths/minute, altered mental status or confusion, extreme pain or discomfort ('worst ever'), pale or mottled skin, clammy or sweaty skin, and feeling that something is seriously wrong. The Sepsis-3 criteria define septic shock by the need for vasopressors and elevated lactate. Treatment requires urgent hospital admission, intravenous antibiotics within the first hour ('one-hour bundle'), IV fluids, oxygen, and organ support. Time is critical — mortality increases significantly with each hour of delay.

title: Anaphylaxis: Symptoms and Emergency Response
content: Anaphylaxis is a severe, life-threatening allergic reaction that occurs rapidly — usually within minutes — after exposure to an allergen such as food (peanuts, tree nuts, shellfish, milk, eggs), insect stings (bee, wasp), medications (penicillin, NSAIDs, contrast dye), or latex. It involves multiple organ systems simultaneously. Symptoms include skin reactions (hives, itching, flushed or pale skin), swelling of the throat and tongue causing difficulty swallowing or breathing, wheezing or stridor, a rapid or weak pulse, severe drop in blood pressure, dizziness or fainting, nausea, vomiting, and abdominal cramping. Anaphylaxis is a medical emergency. First-line treatment is intramuscular epinephrine (adrenaline), ideally administered into the outer thigh. All people at risk should carry a prescribed epinephrine auto-injector (EpiPen) and call emergency services immediately after using it.

title: Hypothermia and Frostbite: Symptoms and Overview
content: Hypothermia occurs when the body loses heat faster than it can produce it, causing core body temperature to drop below 35°C (95°F). Mild hypothermia (32-35°C) causes shivering, numbness, poor coordination, slurred speech, and confusion. Moderate to severe hypothermia (<32°C) involves loss of shivering, severe confusion, difficulty moving, slow or absent breathing, and cardiac arrhythmias. It is a medical emergency. Frostbite is injury to body tissues from freezing, most commonly affecting fingers, toes, nose, ears, and cheeks. Superficial frostbite (frostnip) causes numbness, white or grayish-yellow skin, and hard or waxy texture. Deep frostbite causes complete numbness, blistering, and tissue death. First aid includes moving to a warm environment, removing wet clothing, and rewarming — but do not rub affected areas or rewarm if refreezing is possible.

title: Obesity: Health Risks and Overview
content: Obesity is defined as excessive body fat accumulation, classified as a body mass index (BMI) of 30 kg/m² or above, with class III (severe) obesity at 40 kg/m² or above. Obesity significantly increases the risk of a wide range of health conditions: type 2 diabetes, hypertension, coronary heart disease, heart failure, stroke, obstructive sleep apnea, osteoarthritis, non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD/NASH), gallstones, several cancers (breast, colon, endometrial, kidney, esophageal), and depression. The condition results from a complex interaction of genetics, diet, physical activity, sleep, stress, medications, and socioeconomic factors — it is not simply a matter of willpower. Evidence-based management includes dietary modification, increased physical activity, behavioral interventions, anti-obesity medications (orlistat, GLP-1 receptor agonists such as semaglutide), and, for eligible patients, bariatric surgery.

title: Opioid Use Disorder: Symptoms and Overview
content: Opioid use disorder (OUD) is a chronic medical condition characterized by compulsive use of opioids (heroin, fentanyl, prescription painkillers like oxycodone or hydrocodone) despite significant negative consequences. Behavioral signs include using more opioids than intended or for longer than intended, unsuccessful attempts to cut down, spending excessive time obtaining or using opioids, craving, failure to fulfill work or family obligations, and continued use despite knowing harms. Physical signs of acute intoxication include drowsiness, constricted pupils (miosis), slurred speech, and slowed breathing. Opioid overdose — characterized by unconsciousness, pinpoint pupils, and respiratory depression (slow, shallow, or absent breathing) — is a medical emergency treatable with naloxone (Narcan). Evidence-based treatment of OUD includes medications (methadone, buprenorphine-naloxone, extended-release naltrexone) combined with behavioral counseling.

title: Liver Cirrhosis: Symptoms and Overview
content: Cirrhosis is the late stage of progressive liver fibrosis, in which normal liver tissue is replaced by scar tissue, impairing liver function. Major causes include chronic alcohol use disorder, chronic hepatitis B and C infection, and non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD). Early (compensated) cirrhosis may be asymptomatic. As it progresses, symptoms include fatigue, weakness, loss of appetite, nausea, weight loss, and abdominal discomfort. Decompensated cirrhosis presents with jaundice (yellow skin and eyes), ascites (fluid accumulation in the abdomen), peripheral edema, esophageal varices (enlarged veins that can bleed), hepatic encephalopathy (confusion, drowsiness, coma from toxin buildup), and increased susceptibility to infections. Cirrhosis is irreversible, but its progression can be slowed by treating the underlying cause. Liver transplantation is the only cure for end-stage disease.

title: HIV and AIDS: Symptoms and Overview
content: HIV (human immunodeficiency virus) attacks and destroys CD4+ T cells (helper T cells), weakening the immune system. HIV is transmitted through blood, semen, vaginal fluids, rectal fluids, and breast milk — primarily through unprotected sex, sharing needles, or mother-to-child transmission. Acute HIV infection (2-4 weeks after exposure) may cause a flu-like illness (fever, swollen lymph nodes, sore throat, rash, muscle aches — 'acute retroviral syndrome') that resolves spontaneously. Many people then remain asymptomatic for years. Without treatment, the immune system progressively declines until CD4 count falls below 200 cells/µL, at which point AIDS is diagnosed. AIDS is defined by severe immune deficiency and susceptibility to opportunistic infections (Pneumocystis pneumonia, CMV retinitis, cryptococcal meningitis) and AIDS-defining cancers (Kaposi sarcoma). Antiretroviral therapy (ART) — started early, taken lifelong — suppresses the virus, preserves immune function, and prevents AIDS. Pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) prevents HIV acquisition in high-risk individuals.

title: Epilepsy and Seizures: Symptoms and Overview
content: Epilepsy is a neurological disorder characterized by recurrent, unprovoked seizures — sudden, uncontrolled bursts of electrical activity in the brain. There are many seizure types. Generalized tonic-clonic seizures (formerly 'grand mal') involve sudden loss of consciousness, body stiffening (tonic phase) followed by rhythmic jerking (clonic phase), lasting 1-3 minutes, often followed by confusion and fatigue (postictal state). Absence seizures (formerly 'petit mal') are brief (2-15 seconds) episodes of staring and unresponsiveness, common in children. Focal (partial) seizures start in one area of the brain; simple focal seizures preserve consciousness; complex focal seizures impair it. First seizure-like episodes require urgent medical evaluation. During a generalized seizure, keep the person safe (protect from injury, do not restrain, do not put anything in the mouth), place them in the recovery position after convulsions stop, and call emergency services if the seizure lasts more than 5 minutes (status epilepticus).

title: Thyroid Cancer: Symptoms and Overview
content: Thyroid cancer originates in the thyroid gland. The most common types are differentiated thyroid cancers: papillary thyroid cancer (most common, ~85%) and follicular thyroid cancer, both of which have an excellent prognosis when caught early. More aggressive types include medullary thyroid cancer and anaplastic thyroid cancer (rare but rapidly fatal). Most thyroid cancers present as a painless lump or nodule in the neck, often discovered incidentally on imaging. Other symptoms include a change in voice or hoarseness, difficulty swallowing, swollen lymph nodes in the neck, and rarely neck pain radiating to the ear. Most thyroid nodules are benign — ultrasound and fine-needle aspiration (FNA) biopsy are used to evaluate suspicious nodules. Treatment typically involves surgical removal (thyroidectomy), often followed by radioactive iodine therapy and lifelong thyroid hormone replacement.

title: Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD): Symptoms and Overview
content: ADHD is a neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by persistent patterns of inattention, hyperactivity-impulsivity, or both, that interfere with daily functioning. Inattention symptoms include difficulty sustaining attention on tasks or play, frequent careless mistakes, seeming not to listen when spoken to directly, failing to follow through on instructions, difficulty organizing tasks, avoiding tasks requiring sustained mental effort, frequently losing things, being easily distracted, and forgetfulness. Hyperactivity-impulsivity symptoms include fidgeting, inability to stay seated, running or climbing in inappropriate situations, excessive talking, blurting out answers, difficulty waiting turns, and interrupting others. ADHD commonly persists into adulthood, where hyperactivity may diminish but inattention and impulsivity often continue. Diagnosis requires symptoms present before age 12, across multiple settings, and causing functional impairment. Evidence-based treatments include behavioral therapy, parent training, school accommodations, and stimulant medications (methylphenidate, amphetamines) or non-stimulants (atomoxetine).

title: Acne Vulgaris: Symptoms and Overview
content: Acne vulgaris is the most common skin condition, occurring when hair follicles become clogged with sebum (skin oil) and dead skin cells. It primarily affects the face, back, chest, and shoulders. Types of acne lesions include comedones (blackheads — open, oxidized plugs; whiteheads — closed plugs), papules (small red, tender bumps), pustules (papules with pus), nodules (large, painful lumps deep in the skin), and cysts (painful, pus-filled lumps that can cause scarring). Contributing factors include excess sebum production (driven by androgens), Cutibacterium acnes bacteria, follicular hyperkeratinization, and inflammation. Acne is most common during puberty but affects all age groups. Mild-to-moderate acne is treated with topical retinoids, benzoyl peroxide, salicylic acid, or topical antibiotics. Moderate-to-severe or scarring acne may require oral antibiotics, hormonal therapy (for women), or isotretinoin.

title: Dehydration: Symptoms and Management
content: Dehydration occurs when the body loses more fluids than it takes in, impacting normal function. Causes include insufficient fluid intake, excessive sweating, fever, vomiting, diarrhea, and frequent urination (as in poorly controlled diabetes). Mild-to-moderate symptoms include increased thirst, dry mouth, dark yellow urine, decreased urine output, fatigue, dizziness or lightheadedness, headache, and dry skin. Severe dehydration symptoms include very dark or no urine output, extreme fatigue, rapid heartbeat, rapid breathing, sunken eyes, confusion, and fainting — this requires emergency medical care. In infants, signs include no wet diapers for 3+ hours, dry mouth and tongue, sunken fontanelle, and no tears when crying. Oral rehydration solutions (ORS), which contain the right balance of water, sugar, and electrolytes (sodium, potassium), are the cornerstone of treatment for mild-to-moderate dehydration, especially in children with diarrhea.

title: Osteoporosis: Symptoms and Overview
content: Osteoporosis is a metabolic bone disease in which bone density and quality are reduced, making bones porous and fragile and significantly increasing the risk of fractures. It is often called a 'silent disease' because bone loss progresses without symptoms until a fracture occurs. The most common fragility fractures are of the vertebrae (spine — often occurring without major trauma, causing back pain and loss of height), hip, and wrist. Risk factors include older age, female sex (particularly post-menopausal women due to estrogen loss), white or Asian ethnicity, low body weight, family history, low calcium and vitamin D intake, sedentary lifestyle, smoking, excessive alcohol, and certain medications (long-term corticosteroids). Diagnosis is by DEXA scan (dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry) measuring bone mineral density (BMD). Treatment includes calcium and vitamin D supplementation, weight-bearing exercise, and antiresorptive medications (bisphosphonates such as alendronate, denosumab).
